title: Paper Panics
subtitle: Twelve Financial Manias, Runs, and Liquidity Crashes
profile: C: Decision Theory, Economics & Institutional Mechanics

chapters.title: The Winter Option in Haarlem
chapters.subtitle: Why Turning Tulip Contracts into Penalty-Free Options Sparked the 1637 Frenzy
chapters.historical_anchor: November 1636 to February 3, 1637 in Haarlem and Alkmaar, when a Dutch florists' guild proposal to let buyers cancel forward bulb contracts for a 3.5 percent fee converted binding debt into asymmetric call options and drove tulip prices up tenfold in ten weeks.
chapters.exit_fact: When the tulip fever broke at a Haarlem tavern auction on February 3, 1637, not a single bulb had changed hands in the winter taverns and the wider Dutch economy grew without interruption.

chapters.title: The Rue Quincampoix Printing Press
chapters.subtitle: John Law's Debt-for-Equity Swap and the Day Paper Pegged to Stock Collapsed
chapters.historical_anchor: 1716 to May 1720 in Paris, where Scottish monetary theorist John Law merged the Banque Royale with the Mississippi Company to swap two billion livres of French royal war debt into equity—before making the fatal error of pegging paper currency directly to the company's share price.
chapters.exit_fact: After the Prince de Conti sent three wagons to the Banque Royale in May 1720 to redeem paper notes for silver coin, French food prices doubled in six months and John Law fled Paris with only eight hundred louis d'or in his pocket.

chapters.title: The Bookseller of Exchange Alley
chapters.subtitle: How Thomas Guy Cashed Out of the South Sea Bubble While Isaac Newton Doubled Down
chapters.historical_anchor: April to September 1720 in London's Exchange Alley—John Blunt's South Sea Company lending investors money against their own shares to inflate the stock from £128 to £1,000, while 76-year-old bookseller Thomas Guy sold out in six disciplined tranches between £300 and £600.
chapters.exit_fact: While Isaac Newton re-entered the market near the summer peak and lost twenty thousand pounds, Thomas Guy used his £234,000 cash profit to construct and endow Guy's Hospital in Southwark before the stock collapsed to £124.

chapters.title: Black Friday on Lombard Street
chapters.subtitle: The Collapse of Overend Gurney and the Rule of the Lender of Last Resort
chapters.historical_anchor: May 10, 1866 in the City of London, when the giant discount house Overend, Gurney & Co. suspended payment on £11 million of liabilities after hiding rotten railway and steamship loans, prompting Walter Bagehot to formulate the central banking rule of Lombard Street.
chapters.exit_fact: Once Prime Minister Gladstone suspended the gold-backing ceiling of the Bank Charter Act on the evening of May 11 and the Bank of England lent £4 million at a punitive ten percent rate, the street run halted without a single note being printed beyond the legal limit.

chapters.title: The Locked Library on Thirty-Sixth Street
chapters.subtitle: Shadow Trust Companies and How J. P. Morgan Stopped the Run of 1907
chapters.historical_anchor: October 21 to November 4, 1907 in Manhattan—after a failed corner on United Copper shares triggered a run on the unregulated Knickerbocker Trust Company, J. Pierpont Morgan audited the Trust Company of America overnight and locked New York's bank presidents inside his library until 4:45 a.m.
chapters.exit_fact: Realizing that the American financial system had survived only because one seventy-year-old private banker held the keys to his library door, Congress convened the Aldrich Commission and created the Federal Reserve System in December 1913.

chapters.title: The Wheelbarrow Mark
chapters.subtitle: Thirty Paper Mills, Exploding Velocity, and the Overnight Miracle of the Rentenmark
chapters.historical_anchor: August to November 15, 1923 in Weimar Berlin, where Reichsbank President Rudolf Havenstein ran 30 paper mills and 1,783 printing presses day and night to print 4.2 trillion marks to the dollar, until Hjalmar Schacht halted central-bank bill discounting and issued the land-backed Rentenmark.
chapters.exit_fact: At the peak of hyperinflation in October 1923, workers spent their wages so fast that the entire paper currency of Germany was worth less in gold than one-tenth of the pre-war coin supply.

chapters.title: The Ten-Percent Margin Trap
chapters.subtitle: Call-Money Loans and Why Paying Down Debt Deepened the Crash of 1929
chapters.historical_anchor: October 24–29, 1929 on the New York Stock Exchange, when $8.5 billion in overnight call-money broker loans hit forced margin liquidation, analyzed by Yale economist Irving Fisher in his 1933 Debt-Deflation Theory after losing $10 million of his own fortune.
chapters.exit_fact: Between October 1929 and March 1933, American borrowers paid off twenty percent of their nominal dollar debts, yet because forced liquidation drove the price level down by forty percent, every remaining dollar of debt weighed thirty-three percent more in real terms.

chapters.title: Silver Rule Seven
chapters.subtitle: How the Hunt Brothers Cornered Two Hundred Million Ounces and Lost to a Rule Change
chapters.historical_anchor: 1979 to March 27, 1980 ('Silver Thursday') in Dallas and New York, where Nelson Bunker Hunt and William Herbert Hunt cornered one-third of the world's deliverable silver at $50.35 an ounce until COMEX Chairman Michel Marks enacted liquidation-only trading under Silver Rule 7.
chapters.exit_fact: Once COMEX prohibited new long buyers and raised margin requirements to seventy-five thousand dollars per contract, silver plunged from fifty dollars to ten dollars and eighty cents, forcing the Hunts to pledge their Placid Oil empire for a $1.1 billion rescue loan.

chapters.title: The Doomsday Machine of Black Monday
chapters.subtitle: How Automated Portfolio Insurance Turned a Dip into a Twenty-Two Percent Crash
chapters.historical_anchor: Monday, October 19, 1987 in Chicago and New York, when computerized portfolio-insurance algorithms designed by Hayne Leland, Mark Rubinstein, and John O'Brien mechanically dumped S&P 500 futures into a falling market and drove the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 508 points.
chapters.exit_fact: Because dynamic delta-hedging requires selling shares whenever prices fall, the sixty billion dollars of insured pension portfolios acted as a synchronized mechanical seller that overwhelmed every human buyer on the floor in five hours.

chapters.title: The Broken Pound on Black Wednesday
chapters.subtitle: George Soros, the Impossible Trinity, and the Ten-Billion-Dollar Wager Against the Bank of England
chapters.historical_anchor: September 15–16, 1992 in London and New York, when Stanley Druckenmiller and George Soros shorted $10 billion of British pounds pegged at 2.95 Deutsche Marks in the European Exchange Rate Mechanism, forcing Chancellor Norman Lamont out of the peg by 7:40 p.m.
chapters.exit_fact: While the Bank of England burned through twenty-seven billion dollars of reserves and hiked interest rates to fifteen percent in a single morning, Britain's exit from the peg lowered borrowing costs and launched sixteen consecutive years of economic expansion.

chapters.title: Account Five Eights in Singapore
chapters.subtitle: Nick Leeson, Short Straddles, and the Earthquake That Brought Down Barings Bank
chapters.historical_anchor: July 1992 to February 26, 1995 on the Singapore International Monetary Exchange, where twenty-seven-year-old trader Nick Leeson hid losing Nikkei 225 futures bets inside secret error account 88888 and sold 37,000 short straddles right before the January 17, 1995 Kobe earthquake.
chapters.exit_fact: When the Kobe earthquake knocked the Nikkei index down past eighteen thousand points, Leeson's unhedged futures and option losses reached £827 million—twice the entire equity capital of 233-year-old Barings Bank, which was sold to ING for one pound.

chapters.title: The Hot-Potato Algorithm
chapters.subtitle: How a Volume-Pegged Sell Order Erased a Trillion Dollars in Thirty-Six Minutes
chapters.historical_anchor: May 6, 2010 between 2:32 p.m. and 3:08 p.m. Eastern Time, when a Waddell & Reed mutual fund execution algorithm programmed to sell 75,000 E-Mini S&P 500 contracts at nine percent of rolling one-minute volume locked into a high-frequency feedback loop until a five-second CME pause halted trading.
chapters.exit_fact: During a single fourteen-second window at 2:45 p.m., high-frequency trading firms passed twenty-seven thousand futures contracts back and forth while changing their net inventory by fewer than two hundred contracts.
